actions.body: Research into autonomous problem formulation reveals that independent discovery requires more than execution capabilities; it demands three foundational pillars: the ability to self-generate goals, mechanisms for self-healing during iterative failure loops, and meta-strategies for resource-constrained exploration. Evidence indicates that agents utilizing self-generated goals significantly accelerate skill acquisition (source-8a1be7f003b94168) and that self-healing mechanisms are critical when systems encounter cascading dependencies in complex research (source-fbe27dc230874d96). Furthermore, the paradox of unconstrained learning suggests that without adaptive meta-strategies, artificial systems default to inefficient exploration, necessitating intentional prioritization (source-c38a2230f18a448b). Together, these findings support the feasibility of autonomous agents identifying significant problems in open-ended environments. Summary: Autonomous discovery systems face critical challenges in iterative experiment refinement and independent goal generation. Success in autonomous inquiry requires robust self-healing mechanisms to navigate failure loops, adaptive meta-strategies for resource-constrained exploration, and mechanisms for self-generated goals to accelerate skill acquisition in unpredictable environments.
actions.lede: Autonomous systems are evolving beyond pre-assigned tasks by integrating self-generated goals and iterative self-healing mechanisms, paving the way for open-ended scientific discovery.

Such measures are used late in the design process and can result in expensive alterations when problems are discovered. Our goal in this work is to provide a quantitative workload measure for use early in the design process. We leverage research in human cognition to define metrics that can measure workload on belief-desire-intentions based multi-agent systems.
